content.text:
The first notice appeared on the school gate on a Tuesday morning. By afternoon, three more copies had been nailed to wooden posts around Adara: PROPOSED EASTERN MARKET ACCESS ROAD. The drawing beneath the words showed a broad grey line passing straight through the village square. At the center of that square stood the oldest baobab anyone could remember.

Nneka read the notice twice. The new road promised a shorter journey to the district market, safer passage for trucks and work for local builders. None of those promises seemed foolish. She had watched her uncle's tomatoes spoil during a week when the old road became nearly impassable. Yet the surveyor's red paint ran across the roots where children sat after school, where elders settled disputes and where the annual planting ceremony began.

At home, Mama Uduak was sorting dried okra when Nneka asked whether the tree could really be removed. Her grandmother did not answer immediately. She put down the basket, fetched a tin key from the seam of her wrapper and opened a chest beneath the bed. Inside were faded photographs, folded papers and a hand-drawn map whose corners had softened with age.

'Your grandfather carried this when the village argued about the land,' she said. A blue line curved behind the baobab and disappeared toward a cluster of farms. Beside the tree someone had written: Common ground—consult before alteration.

Nneka traced the words with one finger. She had imagined the road dispute as a simple choice between saving a tree and destroying it. The map suggested something more complicated: a history of decisions she did not yet understand.

'If this is important, why has nobody mentioned it?' she asked.

Mama Uduak folded the map carefully. 'Some people remember. Others remember differently. And some have never been asked.'

Outside, the first survey stakes stood against the evening light. Nneka took a photograph of the map, but her grandmother insisted that the original remain in its sleeve. The next morning, Nneka would ask Malik to help her find out what the blue line meant.

content.text:
Malik studied the photograph on Nneka's phone while they waited for the school library to open. He was good at noticing what other people overlooked. 'This line could be a stream,' he said, 'but it could also be a boundary or an old footpath. We need the legend.'

The librarian directed them to a cabinet of district maps and agricultural bulletins. After an hour, they found a survey from decades earlier. A narrow seasonal watercourse crossed the eastern edge of Adara, and a shaded area indicated land that became wet after heavy rains. The baobab stood near the margin. In a newer map, the watercourse appeared only as a drainage ditch.

'So the road will flood,' Nneka said.

'We don't know that,' Malik replied. 'We know the land changed. Flooding depends on the levels, the drains, the rain and what the engineers build.'

They took notes on the dates and scales of the maps. Malik insisted they record uncertainties beside every observation. The older survey was not precise enough to settle the alignment of a modern road, and the shaded wet area might have varied from year to year.

That evening, Nneka walked the proposed route with Mama Uduak. Her grandmother pointed to a hollow where reeds once grew and to a stone marker half hidden in grass. She remembered children catching small fish there after the wet season. But she also remembered families struggling to carry harvests to market when the eastern track became mud.

'Would Grandfather have opposed this road?' Nneka asked.

'He would have asked whose land it crossed and who had been heard,' Mama Uduak said. 'He might have supported a road. He would not have liked a decision made behind closed doors.'

In the chest they found a second clue: a receipt from the district records office, signed by Nneka's grandfather and two village representatives. It referred to a land-use agreement deposited with the council.

Nneka copied the reference number into her notebook. The tree was no longer only a symbol of memory. It stood at the intersection of a possible legal obligation, a changed landscape and a genuine need for transport. To understand the dispute, she would have to follow all three.

content.text:
The council archive occupied two cramped rooms behind the administrative offices. Dust settled on the shelves, and several files had been tied with string after their covers broke. Mr. Bassey, the records clerk, searched the register while Nneka and Malik waited.

He found the agreement number, but the folder contained only a cover sheet and three pages. The sequence jumped from page two to page six. Nneka felt a rush of anger. 'Someone removed the parts they didn't want us to see.'

Mr. Bassey looked up sharply. 'You have found missing pages, not a person who removed them. Roof leaks damaged records here for years. We must distinguish what we know from what we suspect.'

Malik wrote that sentence down. They photographed the surviving pages with permission and requested a search of the district duplicate register. The process took several days. During that time, rumors spread that Nneka had discovered proof of corruption. She refused to repeat them, although it would have been easy to gain attention by doing so.

The district office eventually located a certified copy. It described an area of community-managed open space around the baobab and established a process for consultation before substantial changes. It also referred to access routes and public benefit. Nothing in the document imposed an absolute prohibition on roads.

At the kitchen table, Nneka read the agreement aloud to Mama Uduak. Her grandmother closed her eyes at the names of the signatories. Some had been friends; others had been fierce opponents. The agreement had been a compromise, not a perfect settlement.

'Then we cannot say the road is illegal,' Nneka admitted.

'Not from this document alone,' Malik said. 'We should ask someone qualified to explain whether the agreement still applies and how the current proposal affects it.'

The next day they submitted a written request for clarification and asked that the council publish the route alternatives, impact assessments and meeting schedule. Nneka felt impatient with procedures. A bulldozer could destroy the tree in an afternoon; paperwork seemed painfully slow.

But the missing pages had taught her an uncomfortable lesson. A cause worth defending could still be damaged by careless claims. If she wanted the village to trust her evidence, she had to be precise about its limits.

The public meeting filled the primary school hall. Farmers stood near the windows, traders crowded the front benches and young people gathered beneath the ceiling fans. Chief Ekanem opened with photographs of trucks stuck on the old market road. He described losses during harvest season, emergency journeys delayed by damaged bridges and jobs that better transport might create.

A trader named Mrs. Ojo raised her hand. 'My daughter missed a hospital appointment because the vehicle could not pass. I love that tree, but I also love my family. What is your answer?'

Nneka had rehearsed a speech about heritage. Suddenly it sounded inadequate. She thanked Mrs. Ojo and acknowledged that the existing road caused real harm. Then she displayed the old map, the duplicate agreement and the consultation clause. 'I am not asking Adara to reject a road,' she said. 'I am asking why we were shown only one route.'

Engineer Ms. Bello, who represented the project team, explained that the original alignment had been selected for its directness and preliminary cost estimate. Detailed drainage surveys and some land consultations had not yet been completed. Several people shouted that the design was already final. Ms. Bello corrected them: approval depended on further review, but early plans often became difficult to change once expectations formed.

Malik asked whether the team had assessed impacts on market stalls, farms, pedestrian crossings and the old drainage corridor. Ms. Bello listed what had been studied and what remained incomplete. Chief Ekanem looked uneasy when residents requested the reports in language they could understand.

The meeting became tense. Some accused Nneka of delaying progress; others accused the council of selling the village's future. Mama Uduak rose slowly from her chair. 'When we made the first agreement,' she said, 'people argued just as loudly. The point was not that everyone agreed. The point was that everyone had a chance to speak.'

By the end of the evening, the council had committed to a public review of alternatives and an independent assessment of the tree and drainage conditions. The road was neither cancelled nor approved.

Walking home, Nneka admitted she had been afraid of Mrs. Ojo's question. Malik said that fear had helped her listen. They passed the baobab under a moonless sky, and for the first time Nneka saw the village square not as a battlefield between good and bad people, but as a place where legitimate needs collided.

The assessment team arrived with measuring tapes, survey equipment, soil augers and a drone. Dr. Sani, an environmental scientist, invited Nneka and Malik to observe from the designated safe area. The engineers measured ground elevations, mapped drainage channels and documented how water might move during intense rainfall. An arborist inspected the baobab's crown, trunk and rooting environment.

Near the proposed roadbed, a soil sample revealed a darker layer beneath lighter surface material. Nneka immediately remembered the old map. 'That proves there was a wetland.'

'It may support that possibility,' Dr. Sani replied, 'but one layer cannot tell the whole story. We need to examine texture, drainage features, landscape position and other records. We also need to consider how the soil has been disturbed.'

The team compared multiple sampling locations and noted where conclusions remained uncertain. Ms. Bello explained that the design would have to account for runoff from the road surface and maintain drainage routes. Even if the baobab were avoided, construction could affect nearby properties unless those pathways were understood.

At lunch, Nneka asked the arborist whether the tree would survive if the road simply curved around its trunk. The answer disappointed her. Roots extended beyond the visible canopy, and excavation, soil compaction or changes in drainage could damage them. Protection required more than drawing a line a few metres away.

She wrote the findings in two columns: observations and interpretations. The observations included surveyed elevations, measured drainage dimensions and visible root-zone conditions. The interpretations concerned likely flood pathways, ecological significance and design risks. Each interpretation had a different level of confidence.

Later, Chief Ekanem visited the site. He asked whether the investigations were designed to delay construction. Dr. Sani replied that good investigations could prevent expensive mistakes, whether the project proceeded or changed course.

Nneka expected to feel triumphant as the evidence accumulated. Instead she felt responsible. If the revised road harmed households downstream, saving the tree would not be enough. The work had widened her understanding of stewardship: protecting one valued place required thinking about the wider landscape and the people living within it.

content.text:
Three alignments were displayed on large sheets in the school hall. Route A followed the original direct line, reducing travel distance but removing the baobab and disturbing the square. Route B avoided the tree yet crossed a row of market stalls and required several businesses to relocate. Route C used an existing corridor farther east, preserved the square and most stalls, but needed drainage upgrades, safer pedestrian crossings and a longer approach for some vehicles.

Ms. Bello warned that all costs were preliminary. Engineers still needed design checks, permits and a funding decision. The council invited residents to identify impacts that drawings could not show. A wheelchair user pointed out that the proposed crossings lacked accessible details. A farmer explained that the eastern corridor was his only practical route to an irrigation intake. Traders asked how construction would affect deliveries.

Nneka helped organize the comments into a comparison table: travel benefits, construction costs, heritage impacts, flood risks, land access, safety and maintenance. She was surprised when Route C received strong support but not universal approval. People living near that corridor feared noise and dust. Their concerns were as real as hers had been.

At the next meeting, the project team proposed a modified Route C with access protections, revised crossings and further drainage design. Some households would still face disruption, and compensation questions required formal review. Chief Ekanem apologized for presenting the first route before meaningful consultation.

'If we choose this one, does everyone win?' a younger student asked Nneka.

'No,' she said. 'We choose with better information, and we must keep listening to people who carry the costs.'

The council endorsed the revised alignment conditionally, subject to the required approvals and safeguards. Nneka did not celebrate as though the matter were finished. She asked who would monitor construction and how residents could report problems. Malik suggested publishing the commitments beside the project schedule.

That evening Mama Uduak examined the comparison table and smiled. 'Your grandfather would have liked the questions,' she said. Nneka looked at the tree through the window. It was still standing, but the real achievement was larger: Adara had begun to treat public decisions as a responsibility shared by the people affected.

content.text:
The following year, the baobab remained in the square while preparatory work for the revised road proceeded through the required stages. Some promised improvements were still awaiting funding. A drainage inspection identified a blocked section that had to be cleared before major earthworks. Residents continued to argue about dust controls, access and the timetable. Nneka no longer regarded those arguments as proof of failure. They were reminders that decisions needed follow-through.

With Malik and their teachers, she organized an exhibition called Beneath the Roots of Yesterday. One wall held copies of the historical maps; another displayed the consultation agreement and a timeline showing which claims had been confirmed, corrected or left unresolved. Students built a small landscape model illustrating how roads, soil and drainage interacted. Mrs. Ojo contributed a photograph of spoiled produce on the old route and explained why transport mattered to traders.

Mama Uduak told visitors about the square as it had been in her childhood. She did not pretend every memory was exact. When someone challenged the location of the former stream, she pointed them toward the survey records and invited them to compare sources.

The district office agreed to preserve a copy of the recovered agreement in a more secure archive. A community monitoring group recorded concerns during construction planning, and the council posted responses in public. Progress remained uneven, but information no longer depended entirely on private conversations.

On the last afternoon of the exhibition, Nneka sat beneath the baobab and watched children trace the painted lines of the landscape model. A boy asked whether she had discovered a secret hidden under the roots.

'I found an old map,' she said. 'Then I found questions people had stopped asking.'

He seemed disappointed. Nneka understood. She too had wanted a dramatic revelation, one document that would settle everything. Instead she had found disagreements, incomplete evidence, competing needs and the patient work of listening.

She opened her notebook to its final page and wrote: We do not inherit the past as a finished story. We inherit the responsibility to decide what happens next.

Above her, the branches stirred in the evening wind. Beyond the square, the route of the future road curved away toward the farms and the market. Both the tree and the road belonged to Adara's unfinished story.
